text.p: Lithuania's Vytautas Landsbergis, bidding to return to power in elections on Sunday, was the unlikely spearhead of the Baltic state's drive for independence which helped bring down the Soviet empire.

Opinion polls indicate that Landsbergis' Homeland Union has a good chance of emerging from the polls with most seats in parliament, unseating their long-time foes of the ruling former Communist party.

The short and stocky former music professor gained worldwide admiration for himself and his countrymen in 1990-91 as he faced off against a Moscow eager to curb Lithuania and neighbouring Baltic states, Estonia and Latvia.
He had come to prominence with his election as head of the Sajudis independence movement in 1988, when the nationalist cause was still in its infancy.
Sajudis took power in 1990 and Landsbergis became head of parliament the following month.
Spurning the more gradualist approach of Estonia and Latvia, Lithuania set itself on a confrontation course with Moscow. The day Landsbergis was elected, parliament declared independence.
A furious Soviet leadership immediately threw up an economic blockade against Lithuania and the pressure caused Landsbergis to suspend the independence declaration and start negotiations.
Landsbergis held his nerve during the bloodiest incident in the independence drive when 13 people were killed in an assault on the Vilnius television tower in Moscow's hardline backlash.
With the Soviet Union paralysed by a coup attempt in August 1991, the Baltic states made the final break and declared their independence. It was recognised by Moscow the following month.
Although Landsbergis' international reputation was high, at home Sajudis was riven by internal strife as it tried to cope with the collapse of Lithuania's economy after independence.
In a cruel reversal in elections in 1992, Sajudis was defeated by the reformed Communist party, renamed the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP), led by Algirdas Brazauskas.
Brazauskas sealed the comeback a year later by beating the Sajudis candidate in presidential elections.
True to his confrontational style, Landsbergis has spent the years since his defeat sniping at the LDLP, bitterly accusing them of corruption and being puppets of Moscow.
Political commentators expect him to take up the seat of speaker of parliament, in possible preparation for a fight for the presidency against Brazauskas in 1998.
Born on October 18, 1932, Landsbergis is the author of several books, specialising in turn-of-the-century composer and artist Mikalojus Ciurlionis.
